subject: pharmacology
title: Ketamine, Etomidate, Dexmedetomidine and Halothane Hepatitis

steps.tx: **Ketamine** blocks NMDA glutamate receptors and disconnects thalamocortical from limbic systems, producing dissociative anaesthesia: eyes open, reflexes partly preserved, profound analgesia with a cataleptic stare. Uniquely among induction agents it stimulates the sympathetic system, raising heart rate, pressure and cardiac output, which made it the classic choice for shocked and asthmatic patients (bronchodilatation included) and the caution in ischaemic hearts where demand climbs with supply uncertain.
steps.say: Ketamine disconnects rather than sedates, and it speeds the heart instead of slowing it.

left.title: Ketamine signature
points: NMDA antagonism, dissociative state with analgesia
Sympathetic stimulation: rate, pressure and output rise
Airway reflexes and respiratory drive relatively preserved
Bronchodilatation useful in severe asthma

right.title: Ketamine cautions
points: Myocardial oxygen demand rises in ischaemic disease
Direct myocardial depression unmasked in catecholamine exhaustion
Increased secretions need an antisialagogue sometimes
Emergence phenomena colour recovery, below

steps.tx: **Ketamine** blocks NMDA glutamate receptors and separates thalamocortical circuits from limbic ones. The anaesthetic state is dissociative: eyes open, some reflexes preserved, deep analgesia, and a cataleptic stare. Among induction drugs it is the one that stimulates the sympathetic system, raising heart rate, blood pressure and cardiac output, and it also bronchodilates. Shock and asthma are therefore classic indications. An ischaemic heart is the caution, because myocardial demand rises while coronary supply may not keep up.
steps.say: Ketamine blocks NMDA receptors and disconnects cortex from limbic circuits, leaving the patient anaesthetised with eyes open, some reflexes spared, and strong analgesia. Heart rate, blood pressure and output rise, and bronchi relax, which suits shock and asthma. The same sympathetic stimulation can overwork an ischaemic heart.

vis.alt: Ketamine is shown blocking NMDA receptors in a dissociative state with rising heart rate and blood pressure, set opposite propofol.
vis.caption: NMDA blockade by ketamine is contrasted with propofol: the eyes stay open in a dissociative state while heart rate and blood pressure rise. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Emergence delirium** is ketamine's famous footnote: vivid dreams, hallucinations, floating sensations and occasional frank agitation as the patient surfaces, commoner in adults, women, larger doses and those with psychiatric histories. A quiet recovery environment, benzodiazepine co administration and avoiding ketamine in psychosis prone patients blunt the phenomenon. Subanaesthetic ketamine infusions exploit different territory altogether, serving analgesia and, as esketamine, treatment resistant depression under supervision.
steps.say: Waking from ketamine can be a vivid trip; quiet rooms and a benzodiazepine soften the landing.

nodes.label: Risk higher: adults, large dose, psychiatric history
Benzodiazepine cover and quiet recovery reduce incidence

steps.tx: **Etomidate** is the haemodynamically politest induction agent, a GABA A modulator on an imidazole ring that barely touches heart rate, pressure or contractility, which made it the choice for shocked, elderly and cardiac surgical inductions. Its sins are pain on injection, myoclonus that mimics seizures, postoperative nausea, and the big one: inhibition of adrenal 11 beta hydroxylase suppressing cortisol synthesis for hours after even one dose, a controversy that shadows its use in sepsis.
steps.say: Etomidate spares the blood pressure and taxes the adrenal; one dose suppresses cortisol for hours.

left.title: Etomidate virtues
points: Minimal cardiovascular depression at induction doses
Rapid onset, short redistribution awakening
Cerebral protection profile: reduced metabolic rate and pressure
Preferred historically in cardiac and shocked patients

right.title: Etomidate costs
points: Adrenal steroid synthesis suppressed for hours
Myoclonus, injection pain and vomiting
No analgesia whatsoever
Sepsis use debated because of the adrenal effect

steps.tx: **Etomidate** is a GABA A modulator built on an imidazole ring, and it barely moves heart rate, blood pressure or contractility. That haemodynamic quiet made it the induction drug for shock, for elderly patients and for cardiac surgery. The costs are pain on injection, myoclonus that can be mistaken for a seizure, and nausea afterward. The serious cost is blockade of adrenal 11 beta hydroxylase, so cortisol synthesis is suppressed for hours after a single dose, which is why its place in sepsis remains disputed.
steps.say: Etomidate leaves heart rate, blood pressure and contractility almost unchanged, so it is chosen in shock, old age and cardiac induction. The injection hurts, muscle jerks can look like seizures, and nausea is common. One dose also blocks 11 beta hydroxylase and suppresses cortisol for hours, which keeps its use in sepsis controversial.

vis.alt: Etomidate induction is shown sparing blood pressure while adrenal 11 beta hydroxylase is inhibited.
vis.caption: Arterial pressure stays steady as etomidate is given, while adrenal 11 beta hydroxylase, required for cortisol synthesis, is marked as blocked. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Alpha 2 agonist **dexmedetomidine** sedates by quieting the locus coeruleus, producing a patient who sleeps yet rouses to voice and drifts back, cooperative sedation with minimal respiratory depression prized in intensive care and awake procedures. Its bills are bradycardia and hypotension (with transient hypertension if loaded fast), dry mouth, and withdrawal hypertension after prolonged infusions. It doubles as an anaesthetic sparing analgesic adjunct across theatre practice.
steps.say: Dexmedetomidine sedates like natural sleep and spares breathing; bradycardia and pressure set its limits.

nodes.label: Locus coeruleus alpha 2 stimulation reduces noradrenaline release
Rousable, cooperative sedation with spared respiration
Bradycardia and hypotension dose limit the infusion

steps.tx: **Halothane hepatitis** divides into two diseases: a mild, common, self limited transaminase rise after exposure, and a rare fulminant immune hepatitis (roughly one in ten thousand to thirty thousand exposures) with fever, jaundice and liver failure days to weeks later. Trifluoroacetylated liver proteins become neoantigens; risk concentrates in middle aged women, obesity, repeated exposures at short intervals and genetic predisposition, which is why halothane histories are taken before any modern volatile is judged innocent.
steps.say: Halothane hepatitis at its worst is immune, fulminant and remembered; repeated exposures write the risk.

left.title: Mild halothane liver upset
points: Transient transaminase rise after anaesthesia
Common and self limited
Shared in small measure by other volatiles
No long term sequelae expected

right.title: Fulminant halothane hepatitis
points: Fever, jaundice and liver failure days to weeks later
Trifluoroacetyl neoantigen immune mechanism
Risk: repeat exposure, obesity, middle aged women
High mortality without transplant assessment

steps.tx: **Metabolism** predicts the hepatitis gradient: halothane is about 20 percent metabolised, sevoflurane 3 to 5 percent (to hexafluoroisopropanol, not the trifluoroacetyl culprit), isoflurane 0.2 and desflurane 0.02 percent, so immune hepatitis becomes progressively rarer across the modern family though case reports trail even desflurane. Cross sensitivity between volatiles sharing trifluoroacetyl chemistry argues for trigger histories that name agents, not just anaesthesia.
steps.say: The less a volatile is metabolised, the less hepatitis it causes; record the agent, not just the anaesthetic.

nodes.label: Immune hepatitis risk falls across the sequence

steps.tx: **Intracranial pressure** separates the intravenous shelf usefully: propofol, thiopentone and etomidate all reduce cerebral metabolic rate and intracranial pressure, while ketamine's historical ban in head injury (cerebral vasodilatation) has softened under modern ventilation and CO2 control, with neurocritical care increasingly accepting it. Dexmedetomidine barely disturbs cerebral physiology. Examinations still reward the classic answer, ketamine raises intracranial pressure, with the modern caveat as enrichment.
steps.say: Classic teaching bars ketamine in head injury; modern practice hedges, but examinations still want the classic.

left.title: ICP friendly agents
points: Propofol: metabolic suppression, pressure falls
Thiopentone: burst suppression at high dose
Etomidate: similar cerebral protection, adrenal cost
Dexmedetomidine: minimal cerebral disturbance

right.title: Ketamine nuance
points: Traditional teaching: cerebral vasodilatation raises ICP
Modern controlled ventilation data soften the ban
Sympathetic surge may raise cerebral perfusion pressure
Avoid where ICP is uncontrolled and unmonitored

steps.tx: **Assemble the induction choice** by physiology: propofol for the routine and day case, etomidate where pressure cannot fall (accepting adrenal debate), ketamine where pressure must rise or bronchi must open (accepting emergence and demand), thiopentone historically and for burst suppression, each followed by maintenance and the dexmedetomidine style adjuncts. The patient's ventricle, bronchi, brain and adrenal glands vote before the anaesthetist does.
steps.say: Induction is a vote among ventricle, bronchi, brain and adrenals; the agent merely counts it.

left.title: Choose by circulation
points: Hypovolaemia and shock: ketamine or etomidate
Severe asthma: ketamine bronchodilates
Cardiac tamponade physiology: ketamine tradition
Day case routine: propofol clarity

right.title: Choose by brain and gland
points: Raised ICP: propofol or thiopentone tradition
Sepsis adrenal debate: etomidate cautioned
Psychosis history: ketamine avoided
ICU rousable sedation: dexmedetomidine
